mcqs.question: In a reference-counted runtime, what actually triggers an object being freed?
options: A periodic scan that checks every object for reachability
The programmer calling a manual free function
The object's counter being decremented to exactly zero
The object going unused for a fixed timeout period
mcqs.explanation: The free happens the instant the counter hits zero, on whichever decrement caused it — there's no scan and no timeout involved. That immediacy is the entire appeal of the scheme, and it's also the property that a manual free() and a timeout-based scheme don't share.

mcqs.question: In the CPython example, `del w` immediately prints "Widget freed" before the next line runs. What does that demonstrate?
options: Python always frees objects the moment their code block ends
Reference counting frees deterministically, at the exact point the last reference is dropped
CPython batches destructor calls and runs them between statements
`__del__` is called speculatively before the object is actually unreachable
mcqs.explanation: The destructor runs synchronously on the line that drops the last reference, which is the defining trait of refcounting versus a batching collector — there's no block-scope rule involved (objects can be freed mid-block) and no speculative or batched call happening here.

mcqs.question: A tree node holds a strong reference to its children, and each child also holds a strong reference back to its parent. All external references to the tree are dropped. What happens under pure reference counting?
options: The entire tree is freed correctly, since no external references remain
Only the root node is freed; the children leak
Every node's count stays above zero because of the mutual parent/child references, so nothing in the tree is freed
The runtime detects the cycle and frees the tree on the next garbage collection pass
mcqs.explanation: Each parent/child pair keeps each other's count at least at 1 even though nothing outside the tree can reach any of it anymore — that's the defining failure of pure refcounting. Pure refcounting has no collection pass to fall back on; that backstop only exists in runtimes that add one on top, like CPython.

mcqs.question: Why does marking one direction of a parent/child relationship as a weak reference fix the cycle problem?
options: A weak reference doesn't increment the target's count, so it can't be the thing keeping the count above zero
A weak reference is checked and removed automatically once a cycle is detected
Weak references are stored in a separate memory region unaffected by refcounting
Weak references force the object to be freed immediately regardless of other references
mcqs.explanation: The fix works because a weak reference simply never counts toward keeping the object alive, so when every strong reference is gone the count correctly falls to zero even with the weak back-pointer still technically pointing at it. Nothing here involves cycle detection, a special memory region, or forced immediate freeing.

mcqs.question: A team claims switching from tracing GC to reference counting will eliminate their memory management overhead entirely. What's wrong with that claim?
options: Reference counting requires a stop-the-world pause just like tracing GC does
Reference counting spreads real cost across every reference operation (often atomic updates), plus any cycle-detecting backstop still runs its own scan
Reference counting cannot run in a multi-threaded program at all
Reference counting only works for primitive types, not objects
mcqs.explanation: Refcounting avoids the big stop-the-world pause, but it isn't free — every assignment, pass, and return touches a counter, and that update needs to be atomic under concurrency, which is real, constant overhead that can rival a tracing collector's amortized cost. It has no fundamental restriction to primitives and does support multithreading, just at that atomic-update cost.

mcqs.question: Swift's ARC automatically inserts increment/decrement calls at every assignment. Why can't it also automatically detect and break reference cycles?
options: Swift's compiler is not capable of static analysis on object graphs
ARC deliberately runs only at compile time and never touches runtime behavior
Cycle detection would require a collector to trace reachability from roots, which ARC's pure counting mechanism was designed to avoid
Cycles only occur in Objective-C code, not pure Swift
mcqs.explanation: From inside the counting mechanism, a reference that's part of a live, externally-reachable graph looks identical to one that's part of an isolated cyclic island — both just look like "a live reference." Telling them apart needs a reachability trace from roots, which is exactly the mechanism ARC's design avoids paying for; the limitation is architectural, not a compiler capability gap or an Objective-C-only issue.
